# Welcome {.unnumbered}

Most CDISC courses hand you a finished SDTM domain and walk you through
its columns. This one hands you the raw export instead: five files, five
different date formats, one subject enrolled twice. You build the domain
yourself, decide what to do about the duplicate, and defend the
decision.

This course teaches CDISC clinical data standards by building them: you
take raw data from a simulated Phase III trial (codename **GLPX-001**)
and carry it all the way to submission-ready datasets and outputs, in R.

Every claim about a standard in this book is cited to the section of the
Implementation Guide it comes from (`SDTMIG v3.4, §4.4.4`, `ADaMIG v1.3,
§3.3.8`), so you can check it, and so you learn where to look when the
next question arrives.

::: callout-important
### Before You Start: Set Up Your Tools

Go to [**Before You Begin: Setup**](sessions/setup.qmd) and follow the
steps there. This course pins its package versions with `renv`; the
setup session explains why and gets you restored and rendering in a few
minutes. Nothing else in the course will work until you have done this.
:::

## Who This Course Is For {.unnumbered}

- **Statistical programmers and biostatisticians** moving into clinical
  trial work in the pharmaceutical industry
- **R users in clinical research** who need to produce or consume
  CDISC-standard datasets
- **Data managers and researchers** preparing data for a regulatory
  submission who want to understand the pipeline end to end

You do not need any prior CDISC knowledge. The course assumes you have
never opened an Implementation Guide.

::: callout-note
### Scope and level

**This course is** a hands-on build of one trial's data, from raw
export to analysis datasets and outputs, against the versions of the
standards a 2024 study start would actually be held to: SDTMIG v3.4
(with SDTM v2.0), ADaMIG v1.3 (with ADaM v2.1), the OCCDS v1.1
structure for adverse events, Define-XML and Dataset-JSON.

**This course is not** a reference manual, a substitute for the
Implementation Guides, or a survey of every domain and variable. It
builds a small number of domains and datasets properly (DM, AE, LB and
VS, then ADSL, ADAE and ADLB), and teaches you to read the guides for
the rest.

It is also not a statistics course. The analyses here exist to give the
data somewhere to go.
:::

## What This Course Expects From You {.unnumbered}

- **Working R and RStudio**, and comfort running code you did not write
- **Basic tidyverse**: `dplyr` verbs, pipes, and `ggplot2` at the level
  of "I can read this plot's code"
- **No CDISC knowledge**, and no clinical trials background beyond
  knowing roughly what a randomised trial is

Every code chunk is written to be copied into your console and run in
the order shown, against data that ships with the repository.

## How the Course Is Organised {.unnumbered}

**Part 1: Foundations.** Why clinical data standards exist at all,
argued from a real mess in GLPX-001's raw files rather than asserted;
then the trial itself, its design, and what its data should look like
if the design is respected.

**Part 2: SDTM.** The tabulation standard. Observation classes and
controlled terminology, then building DM (identifiers, treatment dates,
the study-day rule), an Events domain (AE), and Findings domains (LB and
VS), including what to do with a duplicate record, a missing unit, and
an implausible lab value. Closes with Define-XML.

**Part 3: ADaM.** The analysis standard. Why analysis datasets are not
just SDTM rearranged, then ADSL (one row per subject: populations,
treatment, dates), ADAE (occurrence data: treatment emergence and
incidence denominators), and ADLB (basic data structure: parameters,
analysis values, and the baseline every change is measured from).

**Part 4: Outputs and Submission.** Tables, listings and figures; the
Analysis Data Reviewer's Guide; and Dataset-JSON.

::: callout-note
### Current status

This book is being written in the open, session by session. **Parts 1,
2 and 3 are complete**, apart from Define-XML. Those ten sessions are
finished: prose written, every code chunk executed against the
repository's data, every standards claim cited and checked.

Still in progress: Define-XML, and all of Part 4. Their pages exist in
the navigation but are outlines rather than sessions, so you will find
them largely empty if you visit them now.
:::

All data in this course is **synthetic**, generated by
[`R/simulate_trial.R`](https://github.com/sufyansuleman/cdisc-with-r/blob/main/R/simulate_trial.R).
No real patient information is used anywhere. The simulator also plants
a small number of deliberate data defects: a duplicated lab record, a
missing start date, a sex value that disagrees between two sources.
Learning to find and resolve those is most of the job.

> Exercises are included in this book. Solutions, extra exercises and
> instructor material are available in the paid tier.
